claims.claim: Le Guin characterises genre writers of her early period as deliberately cultivating an attempt to be styleless, which she treats as a fault rather than a model.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: genre writers deliberately cultivated an attempt to be styleless
claims.page: answer on The Wave in the Mind sentence

claims.claim: Le Guin says that when she creates another world with a society on it she tries to hint at the complexity of that society instead of just referring to an empire.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: I try to hint at the complexity of the society I’m creating
claims.page: opening answers, on the social sciences

claims.claim: Le Guin tells a world-building questioner that event requires location and that where we are affects who we are.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 1, Continued' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: Event requires location. Where we are affects who we are
claims.page: answer to Marion, on world building

claims.claim: Le Guin prescribes passages that describe what the world looks like, smells like and sounds like as the relief that paces an idea-crammed story.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1, Part 5' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: describe what the world looks like, smells like, sounds like
claims.page: answer on stories too crammed with ideas

claims.claim: Adam Roberts writes that the Earthsea books take care to render their world as a believable, lived-in space.
claims.source: Adam Roberts, "Ursula Le Guin, 'A Wizard of Earthsea' (1968)", Adam's Notebook (Medium), 5 February 2023

claims.claim: Adam Roberts characterises the detail in Earthsea as anthropological as much as mythographic, and linguistic as much as geographical.
Adam Roberts observes that Le Guin has a fondness for low walls as boundaries.
claims.quote: Le Guin has a fondness for low walls as boundaries
claims.page: paragraph on the realm of the dead

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich judges that Le Guin's style has become more colloquial and lower-flown, comparing the language of Tehanu with that of the earlier Earthsea trilogy.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote's Song: The Teaching Stories of Ursula K. Le Guin, Conclusion (SFRA, (c)2000)
claims.quote: Her style has gotten more colloquial, lower-flown
claims.page: Conclusion, section on what has changed

claims.claim: Le Guin, in her Response to the 1975 Le Guin issue of Science-Fiction Studies as quoted by Erlich, said the ideas of the Earthsea trilogy are less detachable from the sounds, rests and rhythms than those of her other work of that time.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Response", Science-Fiction Studies (1975), p. 45, quoted in Richard D. Erlich, Coyote's Song, Conclusion ((c)2000)
claims.quote: less detachable from the sounds, rests, and rhythms

claims.claim: Richard D. Erlich credits Le Guin's 1961 story 'An die Musik' with a genius for handling complex issues in a lucid, simple style at the very beginning of her career.
claims.source: Richard D. Erlich, Coyote's Song, Early Works ((c)2000)
claims.quote: a genius for handling complex issues in a lucid, simple style
claims.page: Early Works, section on 'An die Musik'

claims.claim: Le Guin writes that adjectives and adverbs are rich and good and nourishing, and cause obesity in prose only when used lazily or overused.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft, quoted in Nicole Bianchi, '3 Powerful Writing Exercises from Steering the Craft' (2021)
claims.quote: They cause obesity in prose only when used lazily or overused
claims.page: section 2, Practice Eliminating Unnecessary Adjectives and Adverbs

claims.claim: Le Guin advises that when the quality an adverb indicates can be put in the verb itself, or an adjective's quality in the noun itself, the prose will be cleaner, more intense and more vivid.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft, quoted in Nicole Bianchi (2021)
claims.quote: the prose will be cleaner, more intense, more vivid

claims.claim: Le Guin names Somehow a super-weasel, a word that betrays that the author did not want to bother thinking out the story.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft, quoted in Nicole Bianchi (2021)

claims.claim: Le Guin's exercise asks for a paragraph to a page of 200-350 words of descriptive narrative prose written without adjectives or adverbs, using only verbs, nouns, pronouns and articles.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft, exercise quoted in Nicole Bianchi (2021)
claims.quote: (200-350 words) of descriptive narrative prose without adjectives

claims.claim: Michael Swanwick lists archaicisms, false feeling, fake grammar and journalistic prose as the ways Le Guin says language should not be used in fantasy.
claims.source: Michael Swanwick, 'Revisiting Poughkeepsie, Part 2: The Language of the Night', Flogging Babel, 14 October 2010
claims.quote: Archaicisms, false feeling, fake grammar, journalistic prose
